title: Löydätkö kolme ongelmaa?
caption:
Can you spot three problems on this page before the countdown ends?

It is hard, because nothing looks broken. The menu text is too faint to read, the product photo has no description, and the sign-up box has no name. A customer who can’t see the screen well, or at all, gets stuck on each one.

title: What a shop tells a visually impaired customer (alt text)
caption:
Halden, Runa, Lumi, Aalto. Without the photos, could you tell which one is a coat?

Many shops name products like this, so the photo does the explaining. A visually impaired customer who uses a screen reader, software that reads the page out loud, gets the photo’s description instead. If there is none, they may hear a file name, or just “image”.

In this example only one of the four photos has a description. The fix is one sentence per photo in your shop editor’s “Alt text” field: say what it is, the color and the material.

Save this for your next product upload 📌

Video description: A phone opens an online shop with four products. The photos go dark and labels show what a screen reader may say: “IMG_2041.jpg”, “DSC_0098.jpg”, “Grey wool beanie with a pom-pom” and “image”. Three photos are outlined in red and one in teal.

title: Lunch menu with low vision (contrast)
caption:
Light grey text looks clean. For a customer with low vision, your prices may simply not be there.

The video blurs a café’s lunch menu to show the idea. It is a simulation, and real low vision varies from person to person. The pattern holds, though: faint text disappears first, and it is often the text that matters most, like prices, opening hours and the label on a button.

Stronger text helps everyone, including anyone reading a phone in bright sunlight. Low-contrast text was the most common problem WebAIM found on the top one million home pages in 2026: 83.9% of them had it.

Send this to whoever looks after your website.

Video description: A phone opens a café’s lunch menu. The page blurs, and the faint prices, opening hours and button text disappear while the dish names stay readable. Then the faint text turns dark and everything can be read again, even blurred.

title: What an AI assistant reads on a page
caption:
Some customers now ask an AI assistant to find a service or book a time. Can it read your website?

Many assistants read a page through its text and labels, much like a screen reader does. A picture with no description, an icon button with no name and a form field with no label give them very little to work with.

In this example the assistant reads the prices. It misses the offer inside the picture, can’t tell which button calls the salon and doesn’t know what the booking field is for.

Fixing these doesn’t guarantee that an assistant will recommend you. It does make your site readable to it, and the same fixes help customers who use a screen reader.

title: Aukioloajat kuvan sisällä
caption:
When does this shop close on Saturday? Easy, unless you can’t see the picture.

If your opening hours are inside a picture, a screen reader may only read the file name. The same goes for menus, price lists and offers saved as images.

The fix is simple: type the text onto the page. You can keep the picture next to it.

Save this for the next time you update your hours 📌

Video description: Opening hours shown as a picture. The picture goes dark and a speech bubble shows the file name “hours_final.png”. Then the hours are read as text: “Saturday, 10 to 15”.

title: Näyttävät samalta, kuulostavat erilta
caption:
These two product cards look exactly the same. One of them is broken.

title: Etsi puhelinnumero alatunnisteesta
caption:
Find the phone number in this footer. You have three seconds.

Light grey text on a dark footer looks tidy, but it hides the things customers come looking for: your phone number, address and opening hours.

It was the most common problem WebAIM found in 2026: 83.9% of the top one million home pages had text that is too faint.

The fix is often one color code.

title: The page that won’t let you zoom
hook: This text is tiny. So why can’t you zoom in?
caption:
This text is tiny. So why can’t you zoom in?

Some websites switch off pinch-to-zoom with one setting in the page’s code. On many phones the page then stays the same size, however small the text is. For a customer with low vision, that can mean they can’t read your prices or opening hours at all.

The fix is to remove that one setting. Selkeo tells you if your site blocks zoom and how to switch it back on.

Send this to whoever runs your site.

For viewers who can’t see the video: A phone opens a gym’s class timetable in very small text. Two fingers try to zoom in twice and the page stays the same size. A note says zoom is switched off on this page. After the fix, the same gesture makes the text bigger.

title: The page that never says what language it is in
hook: What does this French bakery sound like to a screen reader?
caption:
What does this French bakery sound like to a screen reader?

A screen reader is software that reads a page out loud for a visually impaired customer. To pick the right voice, it looks at the language set in the page’s code.

This page is in French, but it never says so. The screen reader may then read the French words with an English voice, and the result is hard to understand.

The fix is one short line of code. In WebAIM’s 2026 study of the top million home pages, 13.5% had no language set.

Selkeo tells you if your page is one of them. Send this to whoever runs your site.

For viewers who can’t see the video: A phone opens a French bakery’s page. A note says the page never says what language it is in, and a box shows how an English voice may mangle the French greeting. After one line of code sets the language to French, the box shows the greeting read correctly.
